description: Guided manual, AT and user-testing checks. A corpus cannot perform these; it carries the question, the fixture and an evidence slot so the requirement is visible and trackable rather than silently missing from a coverage figure.
note: All cases expect cannot-tell. A scanner reporting pass on these is overclaiming.

cases.question: Do the captions convey the same information as the audio?
cases.notes: A tool can confirm a caption track exists and parses. It cannot judge accuracy, synchronisation, or whether speakers are identified.

cases.question: Does each text alternative serve the same purpose as the image?
cases.notes: A tool can detect a missing or empty alt. It cannot tell whether "image1.jpg" or "a photo" conveys what the image is there to convey — the commonest real failure is alt text that is present and useless.

cases.question: Does the DOM order match the meaningful reading order?
cases.notes: CSS can reorder content visually while the DOM stays unchanged. A tool sees a valid DOM and a valid layout; only a person can say the two tell different stories.

cases.question: Do instructions rely on shape, size, position, sound or colour alone?
cases.notes: Detecting the phrase "the button on the right" is possible; deciding whether it is the ONLY way to identify the control requires understanding the page.

cases.question: Is the content understandable without specialist knowledge?
cases.notes: Readability formulas measure sentence and word length, not comprehensibility. A short sentence of jargon scores well and communicates nothing.

cases.question: Does the focus order preserve meaning and operability?
cases.notes: A tool can record the tab sequence. Whether that sequence makes SENSE for the task is a judgement about the task, not the DOM.

cases.question: Can a screen-reader user complete the task from start to finish?
cases.notes: This is the only check that answers the question the others approximate. It needs a real screen reader and a person who uses one; results do not transfer between pairings, so a pass with one is not a pass with another.

cases.question: Is the AI-suggested text alternative correct for THIS context?
cases.notes: A model can describe what is in an image. It cannot know why the image is on the page, which is what the alternative has to convey — the same photo needs different alt text in a news story and a checkout page. Suggestions are a starting point and must be verified; shipping them unreviewed replaces a missing alt with a confidently wrong one, which is harder to find.

cases.question: Does the sign-language interpretation convey the same information as the audio?
cases.applicability: inapplicable when there is no prerecorded audio in synchronised media
cases.notes: A tool can detect that a sign-language track is present. It cannot judge whether the signing is complete, correctly timed, in the sign language the audience actually uses, or large and well-lit enough to read. Sign languages are distinct languages, not transliterations of the spoken track.

cases.question: Do the pauses allow every important visual detail to be described?
cases.applicability: inapplicable when foreground audio pauses already allow full description
cases.notes: Standard audio description fits into existing gaps in the dialogue. Deciding that those gaps are too short, and that the video must be paused to say more, requires knowing what the picture carries that the soundtrack does not.

cases.question: Is there a live equivalent for the live audio-only content?
cases.applicability: inapplicable when no live audio-only content is presented
cases.notes: The alternative has to exist while the broadcast is happening and keep pace with it. A corpus can hold the question but not a live stream, and whether the equivalent keeps up is judged by someone following both at once.

cases.question: Is the background at least 20 dB below the foreground narration?
cases.applicability: inapplicable to musical performance and where spoken content is incidental
cases.notes: The separation is measurable, but only from the rendered audio, and deciding which passages are foreground narration rather than incidental sound is a listening judgement. Markup says nothing about either.

cases.question: Is a definition available for every word used in an unusual or restricted way?
cases.notes: Whether a word is unusual depends on who is reading. Jargon, idiom and words given a narrow technical meaning all qualify, and none of them is detectable by looking the word up — the same word is ordinary in one audience and opaque in another.

cases.question: Is pronunciation available where meaning is ambiguous without it?
cases.applicability: inapplicable where no word is ambiguous without its pronunciation
cases.notes: The criterion applies only where the word cannot be understood without knowing how it is said. Deciding that a heteronym is genuinely ambiguous in its context, rather than resolved by the surrounding sentence, is a reading judgement.

cases.question: Can people with disabilities actually complete this task?
cases.notes: Conformance is not usability. A page can meet every criterion and still be unusable, and the only way to find that out is to watch people try. No corpus, and no tool, substitutes for this.
